1
INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
The Florida Prosecuting Attorneys Association,
Inc., (“FPAA”), is a nonprofit corporation whose members are the twenty elected State Attorneys as well as
over two-thousand Assistant State Attorneys.  It was
created to serve the needs of prosecutors and the administration of justice as prescribed by the Florida
Constitution and laws of Florida. The FPAA submits
this brief as an  Amicus Curiae in support of the  Respondent, the State of Florida, and in the interest of
the administration of justice nationwide.
1

As the prosecutors of all criminal offenses in trial
court in the State of Florida, the FPAA’s membership
would be directly and negatively impacted by any
opinion of this Court that would overturn its long -
standing precedent recognizing the constitutionality
of Florida’s use of six-member juries.
The FPAA supports the decision of the Fourth District Court of Appeal and the position of the Respondent, the State of Florida , and urges this Court to uphold its precedent in Williams v. Florida, 399 U.S. 78
(1970).  Specifically, the FPAA files this brief to address the real-life effects that such a drastic change in
the law would create and to highlight the reliance interests of Florida’s prosecutors and court system.


1
 The parties have consented to the filing of this amicus brief.  No
party or party’s counsel authored this brief in whole or in part.
No party, counsel for a party, or any person other than Amicus
Curiae and its counsel made a monetary contribution intended
to fund the preparation or submission of the brief.

2
SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
First, Williams was correctly decided on the merits.  Over fifty years ago, this Court addressed the
meaning of the phrase “trial, by an impartial jury” in
the Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution.  In doing so, it engaged in precisely the kind of
originalist analysis that this Court has repeatedly required in determining such constitutional questions.

The Williams court examined the language of competing proposals to enshrine the right to a trial by jury
for criminal offenses in the Constitution.  In doing so,
they determined that the intent to decouple the constitutional right to trial by jury from the “accustomed
requisites” of the common law , such as jury size, was
the “more plausible” explanation for the language ultimately adopted by Congress and ratified by the
states.  There is no reason to believe that the Williams
court’s analysis was wrong, and it should not be disturbed here.

But even if this Court were to find the historical
analysis and logical reasoning of Williams to be
flawed, stare decisis mandates that this Court adhere
to its prior precedent .  At the first step, a mere disagreement about the meaning of a constitutional term
is an insufficient basis to find  the precedent “ grievously or egregiously wrong.”

Neither is there any evidence that six -person juries have caused any significant negative jurisprudential or real -world consequences.  There is simply no
reliable empirical data to support the conclusion that
a defendant’s right to trial by jury is better served by

3
juries comprised of twelve than those comprised of six.
To the contrary, the positive real-world consequences
are obvious.  For the very reasons that the Florida legislature chose to set the number of jurors at six for
non-capital offenses in 1877, the financial strain on
clerks’ offices, the judiciary, and th ose citizens called
for jury duty has been significantly reduced.  The current jury-size framework as shaped by Williams and
Ballew v. Georgia, 435 U.S. 223 (1978), functions effectively and without issue.

Finally, the reliance interests of the State of Florida—and its prosecutors in particular—are both myriad and substantial.   There are presently over fivethousand convictions in the appellate pipeline in Florida alone that would likely be affected by the overturning of Williams.  Six other states presently permit
juries of fewer than twelve people for serious criminal
offenses, and the reliance interests of those states
would likely mirror those of Florida.

An influx of appellate claims (and the likely influx
of trial cases remanded as a result) of that magnitude
would create an unworkable burden on the court system as a whole.  Prosecutors would not have the manpower or budget  to handle that number of retrials
within the mandate of the Sixth Amendment ’s right
to Speedy Trial.  The inevitable result w ould be a
windfall to defendants at the expense of society  and
the public as prosecutors struggle with the impossible
demand on their time and resources.

4
ARGUMENT
I. Williams was correctly decided.
Over fifty years ago, this Court held that the Sixth
Amendment’s right to “trial, by an impartial jury” was
satisfied by a jury comprised of six people.  See Williams¸ 399 U.S. at 103.

In claiming that Williams was wrongly decided in
that respect, the Petitioner cites to Ramos v. Louisiana, 590 U.S. 83, 90 (2020), for the proposition that
the appropriate inquiry is to “determine what the
term ‘trial by an impartial jury’ meant at the time of
the Sixth Amendment’s adoption .”  590 U.S. 83, 90
(2020); Pet. Br. at 16.  While the Petitioner is correct
about the appropriate inquiry, he  overlooks the fact
that the Court in  Williams made precisely that determination.  The appropriate question for the Court
is not what the right to trial by jury generally meant
at common law .  Indeed, Williams acknowledged
unequivocally that “the size of the jury at common law
came to be fixed generally at 12 .”  399 U.S. at 89.
To the contrary, the appropriate inquiry is what the
term was intended to mean when it was used in the
verbiage of the Sixth Amendment by the people who
used it.

A. Williams undertook the appropriate
historical inquiry.
First, and most importantly, the Williams court
engaged in precisely the analysis suggested by Ramos.
After a review of the historical record available to it,
the Court determined that “ there is absolutely no indication in ‘the intent of the Framers' of an explicit

5
decision to equate the constitutional and common-law
characteristics of the jury,” and that, “if anything, the
more plausible” explanation for the Framer’s decision
to abandon the substantive language regarding the
“accustomed requisites” of the common law was that
they intended to exclude them and to leave the specifics of jury size to the purview of Congress.  See id. at
96-97.  Only after determining that “ the 12-man requirement cannot be regarded as an indispensable
component of the Sixth Amendment ,” did the Court
turn to which components are indispensable under the
Framers’ intended meaning.  Id. at 100.

It is during that analysis that the Court turned to
more practical considerations —not, as the Petitioner
accuses, in an effort to abandon the original meaning
of the Sixth Amendment, but rather to make clear its
understanding of precisely that original meaning.  See
id. at 100-02.  In that context, the Court focused on
the purpose of the jury trial, which it noted was “to
prevent oppression by the government,” providing the
defendant with “an inestimable safeguard against the
corrupt or overzealous prosecutor and against the
compliant, biased, or eccentric judge.”  Id. at 100 (citing Duncan v. Louisiana , 391 U.S. 145, 156 (1968)).
The Court further noted that  the number of jurors
must “be large enough to promote group deliberation,
free from outside attempts at intimidation, and to provide a fair possibility for obtaining a representative
cross-section of the community” in order to ensure the
right envisioned by the Framers.  Id.

By the plain language of Williams, these were not
the considerations of a court intent on ignoring the

6
plain text of the Constitution.  They were just the opposite: a court’s endeavor to frame —in the clearest
terms possible—what the term “trial, by an impartial
jury” most plausibly meant to the people who drafted
it, the Congress who adopted it, the state legislatures
that ratified it , and by extension, the public whom
they all represent.

B. The historical record supports the conclusion in Williams.
Beyond the historical facts considered on the face
of Williams, there is significant additional historical
record to support its conclusion.

Without revisiting each and every example raised
by the Petitioner and Respondent in their respective
briefs, it suffices to say that—at the very least —the
historical record cannot conclusively refute Williams’s
conclusion.  If anything, the body of references taken
as a whole support its conclusion.  While the Petitioner cites to numerous instances of the acceptance
and use of twelve -person juries in his brief, t he Respondent in turn cites to numerous historical instances of the acceptance and use of juries comprised
of other numbers in its own brief .  See Pet. Br. at 18-
23; Resp. Br. at 10-21.

Among the most notable of the Respondent’s historical references is that of Tredymmock v. Perryman,
3 George Croke, Reports of Sir George Croke  259-60
(Thomas Leach ed. 4th ed. 1793), in which the King’s
Bench clarified specifically that, even at common law,
Parliament had the ability to  alter jury size through
legislative act ion.  It bears specific mention in this

7
context, because it comports precisely with the holding
in Williams: “ Our holding does no more than leave
these considerations to Congress and the States.”  Williams, 399 U.S. at 103.

Also among the most notable references , the Respondent cites  to founding -era discussions and debates regarding jury size as it pertains to both the Article III right to jury trial and the corresponding Sixth
Amendment right .  See, e.g., 2 James Wilson, Collected Works of James Wilson 954 (Kermit L. Hall and
Mark David Hall eds., 2007) (Wilson stated: “[w]hen I
speak of juries, I feel no  peculiar predilection for the
number twelve,” but rather “a convenient number of
citizens, selected and impartial, who . . . try the truth
of facts, on which depend the property, the liberty, the
reputation, and the lives of their fellow citizens.” )
2
; 2
Farrand’s Records 587 , 628  (Madison’s Notes, Sept.
12, 1787)  (George Mason reasoned that “ [a] general
principle laid down on this . . . point[] would be sufficient.” (emphasis added); Nathaniel Gorham noted
that “[t]he constitution of Juries is different in different States.”); 3 Farrand’s Records 298 (Washington to
Lafayette, Apr. 28, 1788).  Likewise, the Respondent’s
citations to founding-era dictionaries support a similar lack of specificity as to any particular number necessary to constitute a jury by definition.  See, e.g.,

2
 The Petitioner suggests that Wilson may have simply meant
“that a petit jury could conceivably be larger than twelve—not
smaller.”  Pet. Br. at 21 n.7.  While that claim is  dubious and
unsupported, it is also irrelevant to the analysis.  The mere fact
that the number supported was different than 12 undercuts the
Petitioner’s argument that the Framers intended the term “jury”
to mean “jury of twelve.”

8
Samuel Johnson, A Dictionary of the English Language (10th ed. 1792) (“[a] company of men sworn to
deliver truth upon such evidence as shall be delivered”); 1 John Ash, The New and Complete Dictionary
of the English Language (1775) (“[a] set of men sworn
to enquire into any  matter and declare the truth according to evidence” ); William Perry, The Royal
Standard English Dictionary (1788) (“[a] set of men
sworn to deliver truth on such evidence as shall be
given before them”); Webster, A Compendious Dictionary of the English Language (1806) (“persons sworn to
deliver truth on such evidence as shall be given before
them”); 2 Noah Webster, An American Dictionary of
the English Language (1828) (“consist[ed] usually of
12 men” (emphasis added)).

These references all support Williams’s conclusion
that the Framers intentionally refrained from permanently enshrining jury size in the Constitution, leaving the issue to the sound judgment of the legislature.
But even if this Court were to be unpersuaded that
they confirm the conclusion of Williams, it should be
equally convinced that the evidence fails to conclusively support the opposing view.

C. The Court’s holding in Ramos does
nothing to  disturb the continued applicability of Williams.
Six years ago, this Court held that the Sixth
Amendment right to “trial by jury,” as incorporated by
the Fourteenth Amendment, mandates unanimous
verdicts in serious criminal cases.  See Ramos , 590
U.S. at 111.  In reaching this conclusion, the Court an-

9
alyzed three separate issues.  First, it looked to discern the original meaning of the word “jury,” as used
in the Sixth Amendment —specifically whether it included unanimity as a necessary hallmark.  Id. at 87-
93.  After determining that it did , the Court then
looked to determine whether its only prior opinion upholding the use of non -unanimous verdicts, Apodaca
v. Oregon, 406 U.S. 404 (1972), was binding precedent
upon the Court.  Id. at 101-03.  Finally, the Court addressed whether, if Apodaca represented binding
precedent, it should be upheld under the doctrine of
stare decisis.  Id. at 104-11.

The Petitioner argues that Ramos not only forms
the basis for, but mandates, this Court’s reversal of
Williams.  To the contrary, not a single step of the Ramos analysis analogically compares to this case.

First, Apodaca failed to appropriately consider the
original meaning of the Sixth Amendment at the outset.  Id. at 93-95.  Rather than attempting to discern
what the Framers meant by the term “trial by jury”
and whether it was understood to require unanimity,
the Court erroneously took to  “questioning whether
unanimity serves an important ‘function’ in ‘contemporary society .’”  Id. at 84.  Williams, on the other
hand, approached the issue exactly as the Petitioner
asks the Court to do today.

As Ramos makes clear fifty years later, “the promise of a jury trial surely meant something—otherwise,
there would have been no reason to write it down.”  Id.
at 89 (emphasis in original).  Rather than turning to a

10
“functionalist analysis” based  on the Justice’s personal opinions of whether the originally intended requirements of the Sixth Amendment “offer[ed any]
meaningful improvement” over an obviously erroneous interpretation ( see id. at 99), Williams sought to
determine exactly what that “something” is.  It’s holding was not that the twelve-person jury’s “costs outweigh its benefits in the modern era, so the Sixth
Amendment should not stand in the way .”  See id. at
94.  It was that the original meaning of the word “jury”
in the Sixth Amendment did not include size as an “indispensable component.”  See Williams , 399 U.S. at
100.

Similarly, Williams is in stark contrast with Apodaca at the second stage of the Ramos analysis.  There
is simply no question that Williams presently stands
as precedent of this Court and is therefore subject to
stare decisis analysis.  Seven Justices agreed to the
holding in Williams, with only one Justice dissenting.
See id.  It was not a “badly fractured set of opinions,”
devoid of any true majority holding.  See Ramos, 590
U.S. at 93 -94.  It did not attempt to employ clearly
abandoned or rejected constitutional theories like
“dual-track” incorporation.  See id. at 94.  A clear majority plainly and unequivocally held that the Sixth
Amendment right to trial by jury did not include the
right to a jury of twelve.

And the final stage of the Ramos analysis results
in equally dissimilar positions of Apodaca and Williams.  Unlike in Ramos, each of the stare decisis factors here weighs in favor of preservation of the Court’s
precedent, as is addressed in detail in Part II, below.

11

The logical approach and constitutional analysis
of Williams share nothing in common with Apodaca.
In that light, it is difficult to see how Ramos could ever
mandate that this Court overturn the longstanding
precedent of Williams.

II. Even if Williams were wrongly decided, s tare decisis mandates upholding its precedent.
Recognizing that “stare decisis is not an inexorable
command,” it requires the Court to “ approach the reconsideration of [ its] decisions  . . . with the utmost
caution.”  Pearson v. Callahan , 555 U.S. 223, 233
(2009) (citing State Oil Co. v. Khan , 522 U.S. 3, 20
(1997)).  As this Court has stated:

Stare decisis plays an important role in
our case law, and we have explained that
it serves many valuable ends. It protects
the interests of those who have taken action in reliance on a past decision.  It “reduces incentives for challenging settled
precedents, saving parties and courts the
expense of endless relitigation.”   It fosters “evenhanded” decisionmaking by requiring that like cases be decided in a
like manner.  It “contributes to the actual and perceived integrity of the judicial process.”  And it restrains judicial
hubris and reminds us to respect the
judgment of those who have grappled
with important questions in the past.
“Precedent is a way of accumulating and

12
passing down the learning of past generations, a font of established wisdom
richer than what can be found in any single judge or panel of judges.”

Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Org., 597 U.S. 215,
263–64 (2022) (internal citations omitted).

This Court’s framing and analysis of the traditional stare decisis factors has been varied over time.
See Ramos v. Louisiana , 590 U.S. at 120-23 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring).  In his concurring opinion in
Ramos, Justice Kavanaugh narrowed the factors he
identified throughout historical opinions into three
broader categories of consideration.  Id.  Those considerations are 1) “is the prior decision not just wrong,
but grievously or egregiously wrong?”, 2) “ has the
prior decision caused significant negative jurisprudential or real -world consequences ?”, and 3) “ would
overruling the prior decision unduly upset reliance interests?”.  Id.

In Dobbs, the Court focused on five similar factors.
597 U.S. at 218; see also Janus v. American Federation
of State, County, and Mun. Employees, Council 31, 585
U.S. 878, 917-18 (2018) (same).  For the sake of simplicity and to avoid repetition, we organize the stare
decisis factors here in terms of Justice Kavanaugh’s
“broader considerations,” but in doing so, address each
of the traditionally examined factors.

13
A. If the Court’s conclusion in Williams is
wrong, it certainly cannot be said to be
grievously or egregiously so.
As addressed in part I. A. above, the Williams
court’s opinion was no exercise in judicial activism.  To
the contrary, it was based upon a well -researched review of the factual record as it pertained to the intent
of the Framers.  See Williams, 399 U.S. at 93-100.

It is only after its determination that the Framers’
intended not  “to equate the constitutional and common-law characteristics of the jury ,” and that, “ the
more plausible” explanation for the Framers’ choice of
words was their  intent to permit  Congress to determine characteristics such as size, that it turned to the
more practical considerations.  See id. at 96-100.  And
again, to the degree that Williams’s practical considerations amount to a “functionalist analysis,” it employed a rationale wholly dissimilar from that of Apodaca, that drew the ire of this Court  in Ramos.  See
590 U.S. at 106.  Williams’s focus on practical considerations were not designed to ignore the plain text and
its original meaning, but rather to clearly define it.
See 399 U.S. at 93-100.

As the Court noted at the time, “‘ the intent of the
Framers’ is often an elusive quarry.”  Id. at 92.  Justice
White stated candidly, “ We do not pretend to be able
to divine precisely what the word ‘jury’ imported to the
Framers, the First Congress, or the States in 1789. ”
Id at 98.  To the contrary, the Court could only give its
best assessment based upon the evidence before it.

14
This Court is again faced with the same quandary.
Even if modern research leads the Court to a different
conclusion as to the “more plausible”  explanation for
the Framer’s choice of words, its effort here is nevertheless to divine the precise intent of the Framers.  To
reach a different conclusion and disagree with the one
reached in Williams would be just that: a disagreement.  And “[a] garden-variety error or disagreement
does not suffice to overrule ” the precedent of this
Court.  See Ramos, 590 U.S. at 121-22 (Kavanaugh, J.,
concurring).

Framed similarly, Dobbs discusses “[t]he nature of
the Court’s error” as one of the traditional factors for
consideration.  See Dobbs, 597 U.S. at 218 -19.  In explaining why the nature of the Court’s error
“weigh[ed] strongly in favor of overruling Roe [v.
Wade, 410 U.S. 113 (1973)] and [Planned Parenthood
of Southeastern Pennsylvania v.] Casey[, 505 U.S. 833
(1992)],” the Court noted that its opinions had “declared a winning side” in a “national controversy.”  Id.
Dobbs reasoned that the nature of the Court’s error
was especially egregious because it “short-circuited
the democratic process by closing it to the large number of Americans who disagreed with Roe.”  Id.

Williams does no such thing.  To the contrary, it
“does no more than leave these considerations to Congress and the States, unrestrained by an interpretation of the Sixth Amendment that would forever dictate the precise number that can constitute a jury. ”
Williams, 399 U.S. at 103.

15
B. There is no evidence of significant negative jurisprudential or real-world consequences resulting from the Court’s
precedent in Williams.
It is unnecessary to rehash here the Respondent’s
recitation of the relevant studies and their conclusions
addressed in its brief.  But they make clear that there
are simply no scientific or statistical studies concluding that juries comprised of six people disadvantage a
defendant in any wa y as compared with juries comprised of twelve.  See Resp. Br. at 41-44.

While Williams stopped short of enunciating the
minimum number of jurors necessary to provide the
trial by jury guaranteed by the Sixth Amendment, the
Court’s opinion in Ballew v. Georgia, 435 U.S. at 243-
45, refined the holding of Williams to requiring that
juries be comprised of at least six jurors.  Certainly,
this clarification of the precedent serves to further ensure that there are no future unforeseen negative consequences.

Some of this Court’s opinions have couched this
consideration, in part, in terms of the “workability” of
the precedent.  See, e.g., Dobbs, 597 U.S. at 280 -81;
Montejo v. Louisiana, 556 U.S. 778, 792 (2009); Payne
v. Tennessee, 501 U.S. 808, 827 (1991).   Certainly, a
framework that mandates an impartial jury comprised of at least six members of the defendant’s community “can be understood and applied in a consistent
and predictable manner.”  See Dobbs, 597 U.S. at 281.

16
While Williams and Ballew have created a workable rule and have resulted in no appreciable negative
consequences, there are significant benefits to society
resulting from the Court’s precedent.  Most obviously,
the cost savings to the public that initially motivated
Florida’s change to the six-person jury in 1877 was realized.  See 1874 Senate Journal 16 (“The largest and
most unsatisfactory source of expense to the treasury
of the State is for jurors and witnesses.” ).  Hand -inhand with the cost savings to the State of Florida is
the cost and time savings to its citizens.  Twelve-person juries require summoning twice the number of citizens for jury duty.  While jury service is the well-respected duty and responsibility of a citizen, it is not
without cost to the individual —not only in time, but
in lost wages, travel expenses, and the like.

To be clear, the FPAA does not suggest that these
considerations are relevant to the threshold issue of
whether Williams was correctly or incorrectly decided.
However, where the stare decisis analysis mandates
consideration of the consequences of the precedent, it
cannot be overlooked that the societal and jurisprudential effects of Williams are demonstrably positive.
3



3
 Of course, one can argue the abstract pros and cons of having
larger or smaller juries.  But such a policy debate is different
from the “jurisprudential or real-world consequences” relevant to
the stare decisis analysis.  In fact, one might suggest that the
Framers were wise to leave such policy debates to the legislature.

17
C. The reliance interests of the State of
Florida—and its prosecutors in particular—are both myriad and substantial.
“Since 1875, the Florida Constitution has allowed
the number of jurors to be ‘fixed by law.’”  Gonzalez v.
State¸ 982 So. 2d 77, 80 (Fla. 2d DCA 2008) (citing art.
6, sec. 12, Fla. Const. (1875)).  “The law first ‘fixed’ the
number of jurors at twelve for capital cases and six for
‘all other offenses’ in 1877.”  Id. (citing ch. 2041, Laws
of Fla. (1877)).  In 1885, the Florida Constitution was
amended to clarify that the number could be no fewer
than six.  Id.

In the 150 years that followed, this Court has done
nothing but validate the constitutionality of Florida’s
six-person jury framework.  See Williams, 399 U.S. at
103; Ballew¸ 435 U.S. at 245.  Florida courts have done
the same, in part relying on this Court’s precedent.
See, e.g., State v. Hogan , 451 So. 2d 844 (Fla. 1984);
Gonzalez, 982 So. 2d at 80 -86; Walling v. State , 105
So. 3d 660 (Fla. 1st DCA 2013) .  In that time, countless defendants have been tried —some convicted and
some acquitted—by juries comprised of six people ,
with absolutely no indication whatsoever that the outcome of trial would have been different if a larger
number of jurors had decided the case.

Florida courts and prosecutors continue to try noncapital cases to juries of six people  today, as they are
required pursuant to Florida law.  See, e.g., Serrano-
Delgado v. State, 392 So. 3d 251 (Fla. 2d DCA 2024) ;
Guzman v. State, 350 So. 3d 72 (Fla. 4th DCA 2022).

18
As the Respondent states, there are 5,200 direct
appeals of criminal convictions currently pending in
the State of Florida.  Resp. Br. at 35.  Of those 5,200,
the vast majority involve appeals of jury trials, which,
with the exception of capital offenses, were tried by
six-person juries.  If Williams were to be overturned,
each and every one of those defendants would have recourse on direct appeal and would very likely be remanded for trial by a new jury.  Unlike the reliance
interests addressed in Ramos resulting from the overturning of Apodaca, where only some of the “hundreds” of cases on direct appeal would be affected (see
Ramos, 590 U.S. at 108), every one of the thousands of
cases in Florida would be affected.
4


As a point of reference, the entire State of Florida
conducted 2,069 felony jury trials during the 2024-25
fiscal year . See Fla. Office of the State Cts. Adm’r,
Florida’s Trial Courts Statistical Reference Guide FY
2024-25 at 3-21.
5
  Given the Sixth Amendment’s guarantee of a speedy trial and this Court’s suggestion that
post-accusation delay becomes “presumptively unreasonable” as it approaches one year, the burden on trial
courts and prosecutors would stand to triple. See Doggett v. U.S., 505 U.S. 647, 652 n.1 (1992).

4
 Of course, the FPAA can speak only to the burden on prosecutors and the court system in Florida.  Without a doubt, that number would be significantly higher when considering the effects of
overturning Williams on all seven states that permit juries of
fewer than twelve people for felony offenses.  And that burden
only increases further when considering all of the states that permit such juries for misdemeanor offenses punishable by more
than six months in jail.  See Resp. Br. at 36.
5
 https://perma.cc/Z5CU-WAUM

19

This level and immediacy of increased burden is
simply untenable.  It would be impossible, given the
staffing and budgets of the State Attorneys —and the
court system in general—to try three times the number of jury trials that are normally tried in a year.  Of
course, that impossibility is compounded by the requirement that these new trials include twelve-person
juries, which impose greater cost on the courts, require larger spaces (not only for individual petit juries, but also for venire panels, and for reporting  and
registration of all summoned jurors) that many of
Florida’s courthouses are unequipped to accommodate, and take more time to empanel.

Sadly, the end result of such a burden is predictable, but unavoidable: prosecutors would have no
choice but to offer significantly reduced sentences that
provide unjust windfalls to criminal defendants.  Of
course, these societally-detrimental results would not
only affect the thousands of cases that are reversed on
appeal as the result of overturning Williams, but also
the tens of thousands of cases that would already be
occupying prosecutors’ dockets as they are hit with the
deluge of trial remands.

Perhaps equally compelling may be the reliance of
the hundreds, if not thousands, of victims who have
already once withstood the trauma and hardship of
jury trial.  These citizens have endured the inconvenience, cross-examination, and in many instances, humiliation, that comes with affording criminal defendants their constitutional right to trial by jury.  Such is
rightfully the nature of our criminal justice system.

20
But it is no small thing to force each of them to endure
it all a second time.
6


Such results are a far cry from the “small price to
pay” at stake in overturning Apodaca.  See Ramos, 590
U.S. at 129 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring).   Like the
other factors, the reliance interests in this case weigh
heavily against overturning Williams.
CONCLUSION
Williams was correctly decided.  But even if this
Court were to disagree , stare decisis mandates that
this Court maintain its prior precedent.  This Court
should affirm.
